q: What are the order and degree of the differential equation d²y/dx² + sin(dy/dx) = 0?
x: The highest derivative is d²y/dx², so the order is 2. The equation is not a polynomial in the derivatives (dy/dx sits inside sine), so its degree is not defined. Reading degree 1 from the power of d²y/dx² is the usual slip.

q: Eliminating the constants m and c from y = mx + c gives which differential equation?
x: dy/dx = m, and differentiating again gives d²y/dx² = 0. dy/dx = m still contains a constant, so it is not the required equation.

q: Which differential equation has the family of parabolas y² = 4ax (a an arbitrary constant) as its solutions?
x: Differentiate: 2y·dy/dx = 4a. Substitute for 4a: y² = 2xy·dy/dx, so y = 2x·dy/dx. Check with y = 2√(ax): dy/dx = √a/√x and 2x·dy/dx = 2√(ax) = y.

q: The family y = A·e^(x + B), with A and B arbitrary constants, has a differential equation of what order?
x: y = A·e^B·eˣ = Ceˣ with the single constant C = Ae^B, so only one constant is essential and the equation is dy/dx = y, of order 1. Counting two letters and answering 2 is the trap.

q: y = sin 2x is a solution of which differential equation?
x: y′ = 2 cos 2x and y″ = −4 sin 2x = −4y, so y″ + 4y = 0. Using the factor 2 instead of 2² gives y″ + 2y = 0.

q: What is the general solution of dy/dx = eˣ·y²?
x: Separate: dy/y² = eˣ dx, so −1/y = eˣ + k, i.e. 1/y + eˣ = c. Check: differentiating gives −y′/y² + eˣ = 0, so y′ = eˣy².

q: Which curve is the solution of x·y·dy/dx = 1 + y² with y = 0 when x = 1?
x: Separate: y dy/(1 + y²) = dx/x, so ½ln(1 + y²) = ln x + c and 1 + y² = kx². y(1) = 0 gives k = 1, so y² = x² − 1. Check: 2yy′ = 2x, so xyy′ = x² = 1 + y².

q: If dy/dx = √(1 − y²) and y = 0 when x = 0, what is y when x = π/6?
x: Separate: dy/√(1 − y²) = dx, so sin⁻¹y = x + c; y(0) = 0 gives c = 0. Then y = sin x and y(π/6) = ½. Integrating to cos⁻¹y by mistake leads to √3/2.

q: If 2y·dy/dx = 2x + 1 and y = 2 when x = 0, what is y when x = 3? (y stays positive.)
x: Integrate both sides: y² = x² + x + c, and y(0) = 2 gives c = 4. At x = 3, y² = 9 + 3 + 4 = 16, so y = 4. Dropping the x term gives √13; forgetting c gives 2√3.

q: If dy/dx = y tan x and y = 2 when x = 0, what is y when x = π/3?
x: Separate: dy/y = tan x dx, so ln y = −ln cos x + c, i.e. y = C sec x. y(0) = 2 gives C = 2, so y(π/3) = 2 × 2 = 4. Writing y = C cos x gives 1.

q: What is the general solution of dy/dx + y = 1?
x: Separate: dy/(1 − y) = dx, so −ln|1 − y| = x + k and 1 − y = Ae^(−x); hence y = 1 + ce^(−x). Check: y′ = −ce^(−x), so y′ + y = 1.

q: A town's population grows at a rate proportional to its size. It is 2000 now and 3000 after one year. What will it be after two years?
x: P = 2000e^(kt) with e^k = 3/2, so P(2) = 2000 × (3/2)² = 4500. Adding 1000 each year (linear growth) gives 4000.

q: A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. 100 g falls to 80 g in one day. How much is left after three days?
x: N = 100e^(−kt) with e^(−k) = 0.8, so N(3) = 100 × 0.8³ = 51.2 g. Losing 20 g every day gives 40 g; 64 g is the amount after two days.

q: A quantity Q grows according to dQ/dt = kQ. When Q = 30 it is increasing at 6 units per hour. Starting from Q = 30, what is Q after 5 ln 2 hours?
x: k = 6/30 = 0.2 per hour, so Q = 30e^(0.2t). After t = 5 ln 2, 0.2t = ln 2 and Q = 30 × 2 = 60. Taking the time to be two doubling periods gives 120.

q: Water drains from a tank so that the depth h falls at a rate proportional to √h. With k a positive constant, which equation models this?
x: The rate dh/dt is proportional to √h, and it is negative because the depth falls: dh/dt = −k√h. Without the minus sign the depth would rise.

q: A particle slows down so that dv/dt = −v², with v in m/s and t in s. If v = 1 m/s at t = 0, how far does it travel from t = 0 to t = 3 s?
x: Separate: −dv/v² = dt gives 1/v = t + 1, so v = 1/(t + 1) > 0. Distance = ∫₀³ dt/(t + 1) = ln 4 = 2 ln 2 m. Stopping at t = 1 gives ln 2.
